strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing genuine limitations of existing RAG approaches for secure code generation
Novel application of program slicing to extract security-focused code examples, achieving 81.5% code reduction
Comprehensive evaluation across four benchmarks, six diverse LLMs, and five baselines with extensive ablation studies
Introduction of SecurePass@k metric that jointly evaluates security and functional correctness
Consistent empirical improvements (4.8% average SecurePass@1 gain) while maintaining 98.7% of original functional correctness
Well-written paper with thorough appendices enabling reproducibility; good experimental design practices
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3) validating contributions of individual components
Analysis demonstrating improvements are pipeline-driven rather than dependent on GPT-4o
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines straightforward applications of existing techniques (hierarchical summarization, program slicing, modified RRF) without significant algorithmic innovation
Unjustified hyperparameter choices: multiple thresholds (4.0, 0.75, 0.65) and 2-hop slicing limit lack justification or sensitivity analysis
Small knowledge base with only 704 vulnerabilities (372 Python, 332 C/C++), potentially limiting generalization despite showing unseen CWE type coverage
Modest improvements (4.8%) with variance across models and no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported
Small security benchmark: CodeGuard+ contains only 94 test cases; evaluation on functional correctness benchmarks doesn't strongly validate security-functionality trade-offs
No analysis of retrieval recall—what happens when correct CWE type ranks beyond top-k? CWE-level retrieval robustness unexplored
Using draft (potentially vulnerable) code to retrieve secure examples counterintuitive; code similarity facet often weakest in ablations (Table 3) yet still included
Modified RRF thresholding appears ad-hoc; missing comparisons with simpler alternatives (joint scoring) or other fusion methods
Missing failure analysis: no examples of failure cases, which vulnerability types benefit most, or false positives in security evaluation
Significant computational overhead (3-5 seconds per problem, 10-12% of total time); mitigation strategies mentioned but not implemented
Reproducibility concerns: GPT-4o (proprietary, closed-source) used for knowledge base construction
Some baselines evaluated on limited model sets (SafeCoder, CoSec) due to implementation constraints; INDICT shows catastrophically poor Pass@1 rates (19.8%), questioning competitiveness
Program slicing algorithm assumes accurate PDG construction; no analysis of handling parse errors or complex code structures; 2-hop limit appears arbitrary

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of limitations in existing RAG approaches for secure code generation
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across 4 benchmarks, 6 LLMs, and 5 baselines with extensive ablation studies
Useful contribution of SecurePass@k metric that balances security and functionality, addressing real gap in evaluation
Thoughtful system design combining LLM summarization with program slicing in hierarchical knowledge base
Strong and consistent empirical results (4.8% improvement) while maintaining 98.7% functional correctness
Excellent reproducibility with detailed prompts, algorithms, and promised code release
Thorough generalizability analysis including seen/unseen CWE types, cross-language evaluation, and dynamic testing (CWEval)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily an engineering contribution combining well-established techniques (summarization, slicing, RRF) without significant methodological advances
Major generalization concerns: only 3.9% improvement on unseen CWE types vs. 9-10% on seen types (2.5x drop), suggesting heavy reliance on memorization rather than generalizable principles
Small knowledge base (704 vulnerabilities, 21 CWE types) with unclear scaling properties; evaluation benchmark contains significantly more CWE types (22-23) than training
Heavy reliance on static security analysis (CodeQL) with known limitations; SecurePass@k lacks severity/exploitability distinction; no human validation of security guidelines
Significant inference overhead (5-10+ seconds per query) from multiple LLM calls with parallelization suggested but not evaluated
Arbitrary design choices with limited justification: 2-hop slicing limit, top-k=4, threshold values (4.0, 0.75, 0.65), temperature=0.2 set without ablations
Vulnerability cause analysis lacks validation—no verification that LLM-generated causes are accurate or comparison to human annotations
Program slicing analysis overclaims: 81.5% line reduction may remove contextually important code, not just irrelevant logic; no comparison to alternative slicing methods
Incomplete baseline comparisons: SafeCoder missing results on larger models, CoSec limited by tokenizer availability, INDICT uses different security tool (semgrep vs CodeQL)
Limited failure analysis with unexplained performance drops (e.g., Llama3.1-8B showing -1.0% on seen CWE types)
